==English==
{{wp}}
{{wikidata lexeme|L73}}

===Etymology===
From {{inh|en|enm|discussen}}, from {{der|en|frm|-}} and {{der|en|xno|discusser}} ({{cog|fr|discuter}}), from {{der|en|la|discussus}}, past participle of {{m|la|discutiō||to strike or shake apart, break up, scatter; examine, discuss}}, from {{m|la|dis-||apart}} + {{m|la|quatiō||to shake}}.

===Pronunciation===
* {{IPA|en|/dɪˈskʌs/|a=RP}}
* {{IPA|en|/dɪˈskʊs/|a=Northern England}}
* {{IPA|en|/dɪˈskʌs/|a=GA,CA}}
** {{audio|en|En-us-discuss.ogg|a=California}}
* {{IPA|en|/dɪˈskɐs/|a=AU}}
* {{IPA|en|/dəˈskɐs/|a=NZ}}
* {{rhymes|en|ʌs|s=2}}

===Verb===
{{en-verb}}

# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[converse]] or [[debate]] concerning a particular topic.
#: {{syn|en|bespeak|betalk|debate|talk about|treat|Thesaurus:discuss}}
#: {{ux|en|Let's sit down and '''discuss''' whether we should have a baby.}}
#: {{ux|en|I don't wish to '''discuss''' this further.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive|obsolete}} To [[communicate]], [[tell]], or [[disclose]] (information, a message, etc.).
#: {{syn|en|apprise|impart|Thesaurus:inform}}
#* {{RQ:Shakespeare Merry Wives|1|3|text=''Nym'': I will '''discuss''' the humour of this love to Page.}}
#* {{RQ:Shakespeare Henry 5|4|1|text=''Pistol'': '''Discuss''' unto me; art thou officer? Or art thou base, common and popular?}}
# {{lb|en|obsolete|transitive}} To break to pieces; to [[shatter]].
#: {{syn|en|busticate|fragment|splinter|toshiver}}
# {{lb|en|obsolete|transitive|colloquial}} To deal with, in eating or drinking; [[consume]].
#: {{syn|en|get outside|put away|Thesaurus:ingest}}
#* {{RQ:Emily Bronte Wuthering Heights|chapter=II|text=When the preparations were finished, he invited me with—“Now, sir, bring forward your chair.” And we all, including the rustic youth, drew round the table: an austere silence prevailing while we '''discussed''' our meal.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1854|author=Samuel White Baker|title=The Rifle and the Hound in Ceylon
|passage=We sat quietly down and '''discussed''' a cold fowl that we had brought with us.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1858|author=James Hogg|title=Titan|volume=27|page=306
|passage=In the first room we entered, a soldier and a man, like a clerk or dominie, were '''discussing''' a bottle of red wine; they immediately sprang up and politely proffered us each a bumper.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive|legal}} To examine or search thoroughly; to exhaust a [[remedy]] against, as against a [[principal]] [[debtor]] before proceeding against the [[surety]].
# {{lb|en|obsolete|transitive}} To [[drive away]], [[disperse]], shake off; said especially of [[tumor]]s.
#* {{RQ:Spenser Faerie Queene|III|I|text=For she was giuen all to fleshly lust, / And poured forth in sensuall delight, / That all regard of shame she had '''discust''', / And meet respect of honour put to flight {{...}}}}
#* {{quote-book|en|author=James Guillimeau [''i.e.'', {{w|Jacques Guillemeau}}]|chapter=Of Gripings and Fretting in the Belly, which Trouble Little Children| title=The Nvrsing of Children. Wherein is Set Downe the Ordering and Government of Them from Their Birth. Together with the Meanes to Helpe and Free Them from All Such Diseases as may Happen unto Them. Written in French by Iames Guillimeau, the French Kings Chirurgion in Ordinary| location=London| publisher=Printed by Anne Griffin, for Ioyce Norton, and Richard Whitaker| year=1635| newversion=published in| title2=Child-birth, or, The Happy Delivery of VVomen. VVherein is Set Downe the Government of Women. In the Time of Their Breeding Childe: Of Their Travaile, both Naturall and Contrary to Nature: And of Their Lying in. Together with the Diseases, which Happen to VVomen in Those Times, and the Meanes to Helpe Them. To which is Added, a Treatise of the Diseases of Infants, and Young Children: With the Cure of Them, and also of the Small Pox. With a Treatise for the Nursing of Children. Written in French by Iames Gvillimeav the French Kings Chirurgion| location2=London| publisher2=Printed by Anne Griffih, for Ioyce Norton, and Richard Whitaker| year2=1635| page2=52| pageurl2=https://books.google.com/books?id=fPk1AQAAMAAJ&pg=RA1-PA52|oclc2=222413128| passage=If too much milke be the cauſe, then the Nurſe ſhall not give the childe ſucke ſo often, nor in ſuch plenty: If it proceed from wind, and that doe cauſe the childe to be thus troubled, it ſhall be '''diſcuſſed''' with Fomentations applied to the belly and navell; and with Carminative Cliſters, which ſhall bee given him, {{...}}}}
#* '''June 15, 1751''', {{w|Samuel Johnson}}, letter in ''The Rambler''
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1642|author=w:Henry Wotton|title=[[s:A Short View of the Life and Death of George Villiers, Duke of Buckingham|A Short View of the Life and Death of George Villiers]]
|passage=Many arts were used to '''discuss''' the beginnings of new affliction.}}
